items.title: Rule of Thirds
items.description: Dividing the frame into nine regions and placing key elements along lines or intersections.
definitions: Create balanced, dynamic framing that avoids dead-center default placements.
rules: Do not use when: When centered symmetry is the stronger statement
Do not use when: Graphic dead-center product locks
decisionRules: Avoid when: When centered symmetry is the stronger statement
Avoid when: Graphic dead-center product locks
commonMistakes: Ignoring thirds then cropping badly later
examples: Subject on right third looking into left look-room

items.title: Golden Ratio
items.description: Composition using phi-based spirals or divisions for organic, classical balance.
definitions: Guide the eye along a natural flow toward the subject with refined proportion.
rules: Use when: Hero product art direction
Do not use when: Fast run-and-gun where thirds suffice
Do not use when: When grids confuse the crew
bestPractices: Use as guiding spiral not dogma
Align subject near spiral calm point
workflow: Use as guiding spiral not dogma
Align subject near spiral calm point

Avoid when: Fast run-and-gun where thirds suffice

troubleshooting: Limitation: Harder to mark on set
recommendations: Use as guiding spiral not dogma

items.title: Leading Lines
items.description: Lines in the scene that steer the viewer’s eye toward the subject or through the story.
definitions: Create directed attention and depth using architecture, roads, edges, and gestures.
rules: Use when: Environments with strong geometry
Do not use when: When lines lead out of frame away from subject
decisionRules: Use when: Environments with strong geometry
Avoid when: When lines lead out of frame away from subject
examples: Corridor lines ending on talent with product

items.title: Framing
items.description: Using foreground apertures—doors, windows, hands, props—to enclose the subject.
definitions: Focus attention and add layered depth with a natural vignette of environment.
rules: Use when: Product within lifestyle context
Do not use when: When frame edges obscure critical branding
decisionRules: Use when: Product within lifestyle context
Avoid when: When frame edges obscure critical branding
troubleshooting: Limitation: Can feel gimmicky if overused
examples: Shooting through shelf gap to product hero

items.title: Symmetry
items.description: Balanced mirroring across a central axis for formal, graphic, or calm compositions.
definitions: Communicate order, power, ceremony, or graphic brand precision.
rules: Do not use when: When energy needs asymmetry
Do not use when: Imperfect sets that fight perfect symmetry
bestPractices: Use tiny asymmetry for life if needed
workflow: Use tiny asymmetry for life if needed
decisionRules: Avoid when: When energy needs asymmetry
Avoid when: Imperfect sets that fight perfect symmetry
recommendations: Use tiny asymmetry for life if needed
examples: Dead-center perfume bottle on mirrored set

items.title: Balance
items.description: Distributing visual weight—tone, size, color, detail—so the frame feels stable or intentionally tense.
definitions: Control comfort vs tension by how elements counterweight each other.
rules: Use when: Interview with set dressing
Do not use when: Ignoring weight until the grade stage
bestPractices: Counter large empty areas with tonal anchors
workflow: Counter large empty areas with tonal anchors
decisionRules: Use when: Interview with set dressing
Avoid when: Ignoring weight until the grade stage
commonMistakes: All weight piled on one side
recommendations: Counter large empty areas with tonal anchors
examples: Talent on left balanced by product glow on right

items.title: Depth
items.description: Creating a sense of three-dimensional space via layers, overlap, scale, and atmosphere.
definitions: Pull viewers into the scene and separate subject planes clearly.
rules: Do not use when: Flat graphic catalog requirements without layers
decisionRules: Avoid when: Flat graphic catalog requirements without layers
troubleshooting: Limitation: Needs space and layered set dressing
examples: Foreground blur leaf, sharp talent, soft city BG

items.title: Negative Space
items.description: Empty or low-detail areas that give the subject room and emphasize isolation or calm.
definitions: Heighten subject importance and leave room for typography or breath.
rules: Do not use when: When empty space feels unfinished without intent
decisionRules: Avoid when: When empty space feels unfinished without intent
commonMistakes: Sensor dust/noise in large soft fields
troubleshooting: Limitation: Can feel sparse if brand expects richness
examples: Small product lower-right with large soft void for headline

items.title: Positive Space
items.description: The occupied areas of the frame—subjects, props, and active visual mass.
definitions: Define what the image is ‘about’ by shaping occupied mass against emptiness.
rules: Do not use when: When positive space becomes clutter without hierarchy
decisionRules: Avoid when: When positive space becomes clutter without hierarchy
examples: Grouped skincare set as one positive mass on clean field

items.title: Headroom
items.description: Vertical space above a subject’s head within the frame.
definitions: Keep portraits comfortable and professional by avoiding cramped or excessive top space.
rules: Do not use when: Intentional extreme crops for style
decisionRules: Avoid when: Intentional extreme crops for style
troubleshooting: Limitation: Platform UI may steal top space—plan safe areas
examples: Medium interview with consistent headroom across cameras

items.title: Look Room
items.description: Horizontal space in the direction a subject is looking or moving (also nose room).
definitions: Give gaze and motion a destination so framing feels open and intentional.
rules: Do not use when: Centered symmetry looks
Do not use when: When closed framing is psychological intent
decisionRules: Avoid when: When closed framing is psychological intent
commonMistakes: Subject staring into the near edge
troubleshooting: Limitation: Too much look-room weakens presence
examples: Talent on left third looking right into open space

items.title: Eye Line
items.description: The height and direction of a subject’s gaze relative to camera and other subjects.
definitions: Maintain spatial and emotional continuity so viewers understand who is looking at what.
rules: Do not use when: POV breaks that are intentionally discontinuous
bestPractices: Keep interview eyeline just off lens unless direct address
workflow: Keep interview eyeline just off lens unless direct address
decisionRules: Avoid when: POV breaks that are intentionally discontinuous
commonMistakes: Camera too high creating unnoticed down-look
recommendations: Keep interview eyeline just off lens unless direct address
examples: A/B interview cameras sharing consistent off-lens eyeline

items.title: Background Selection
items.description: Choosing and controlling what sits behind the subject for clarity, brand, and mood.
definitions: Support the subject without stealing attention or introducing conflicting messages.
rules: Do not use when: Leaving BG to chance on hero frames
decisionRules: Avoid when: Leaving BG to chance on hero frames
examples: Seamless paper for pack; branded but soft office bokeh for interview

items.title: Foreground Elements
items.description: Objects placed closer to camera to add depth, context, or selective reveal.
definitions: Layer the frame and create parallax or discovery without losing the subject.
rules: Do not use when: When FG blocks logo/face critical reads
decisionRules: Avoid when: When FG blocks logo/face critical reads
examples: Out-of-focus glassware FG with sharp cocktail hero

items.title: Subject Placement
items.description: Deciding where the primary subject sits in frame relative to space, gaze, and hierarchy.
definitions: Make the subject unmistakably primary and aligned with story energy.
rules: Do not use when: Random centering without intent
decisionRules: Avoid when: Random centering without intent
troubleshooting: Limitation: Must reconcile with movement and overlays
examples: Product lower-third-safe center-right for vertical social

items.title: Visual Hierarchy
items.description: Ordering attention so viewers see the most important element first, then secondary story points.
definitions: Engineer reading order for persuasion—product, face, CTA, or proof in the intended sequence.
rules: Use when: Ads with multiple claims
Use when: Pack shots with badges
Do not use when: When a single pure subject needs no ranking
decisionRules: Use when: Ads with multiple claims
Use when: Pack shots with badges
Avoid when: When a single pure subject needs no ranking
examples: Bright product hero, softer lifestyle BG, reserved corner for logo
